PR7-F-01.hint: Factor the numerator and denominator completely and cancel the common factors. A factor that cancels completely gives a hole. Then look at the denominator that is left; a factor of it that is still there is a vertical asymptote, and the remaining zeros of the numerator are the zeros. Compare degrees for the horizontal asymptote.
slips: Mixing up holes and vertical asymptotes. A factor that cancels completely makes a hole. If the factor is still in the denominator after canceling, that input is a vertical asymptote.
Counting a canceled factor as a zero of the function.
Finding the \(y\)-value of the hole from the original expression, which is undefined there. Use the simplified expression.

PR7-A-01.hint: When there is no common factor, every zero of the denominator is a vertical asymptote. If the degrees are equal, the horizontal asymptote is the ratio of the leading coefficients. If the numerator has the smaller degree, it is \(y=0\).
slips: Taking the ratio of the constants instead of the leading coefficients for the horizontal asymptote.
Forgetting the leading coefficient in the denominator when the degrees are equal.

items.stem: Consider \(f(x) = \dfrac{-2(x - 2)(x + 6)}{(x - 2)(x - 1)}\). Find (a) any holes, (b) the zeros, (c) the vertical asymptote, (d) the horizontal asymptote, and (e) the \(y\)-intercept.

parts.a: \(x = 2\) is a factor of both the numerator and the denominator. After canceling it, the denominator that is left is \(x - 1\), which is not \(0\) at \(x = 2\), so the factor canceled completely and there is a hole at \(x = 2\). After canceling, the value there is \(y = -16\), so the hole is at \((2, -16)\).
The zero is \(x = -6\) (the other numerator zero, \(x = 2\), is a hole, not a zero).
The degrees are equal, so the horizontal asymptote is the ratio of the leading coefficients: \(y = -2\).
\(f(0) = 12\), so the \(y\)-intercept is \((0, 12)\).
